## 3. Add Your Custom Layers – The “Insert‑Before‑Labels” Pattern

Most basemap styles end with a stack of **symbol layers** (labels, icons). If you simply `map.addLayer(myLayer)` after the map has loaded, your layer will be appended **on top** of everything, which means:
* A `fill` layer will be hidden **under** the label symbols.
* A `line` layer may be drawn but then covered by a thick road symbol layer.
**Solution:** Insert your layer **just before** the first symbol layer (or any other layer you want to stay on top of).

// 4️⃣ Insert it before the first symbol layer (or pass null to append)
**If you already have a style JSON** you can embed the layer directly in the `layers` array, but still place it **before** the first symbol entry. The order in the JSON is the draw order.

Your map is missing **glyphs** (font stacks) and **sprites** (icon sheets) – the two assets a style needs to draw any text or icons.
If the tiles you’re serving don’t contain label layers, you also need a **separate vector source that carries the label layers** (or add them to your own tiles).
Below is a step‑by‑step checklist, the most common pitfalls, and a ready‑to‑copy example style fragment that will get labels back on the screen.
## 1. What MapLibre actually needs to render labels

column3: What it is
column4: Why it matters

column3: SDF‑encoded font files (`{fontstack}/{range}.pbf`)
column4: Text is drawn from these glyph atlases. If the URL is missing or the files can’t be fetched, the text layer silently falls back to “no‑glyphs” → nothing is drawn.

column3: A JSON file + PNG sprite sheet (`sprite.json` + `sprite.png`)
column4: Icons (including the default “marker” and any custom icons) are taken from the sprite sheet. Missing sprites also hide symbols that contain an `icon-image`.

column3: Vector tile layers that contain the label features (e.g. `place`, `road_label`, `water_name`)
column4: The style’s `symbol` layers must point to a source‑layer that actually exists in the tiles. If you generated tiles without those layers, the symbol layers have nothing to draw.

column3: `Access‑Control‑Allow‑Origin: *` (or your domain) on the glyph/sprite/tile endpoints
column4: Browsers block cross‑origin requests without CORS, resulting in “Failed to load …” errors in the console and blank labels.

column1: If any one of the above is missing, the map will render the geometry (roads, polygons, etc.) but **no text or icons**.

column3: How to verify
Open the style JSON (or the URL you passed to `map.setStyle`) and look for `""glyphs"": ""…/{fontstack}/{range}.pbf""`.
Paste a concrete URL into the browser, e.g. `https://my.cdn.com/fonts/Open+Sans%20Regular/0-255.pbf`. You should get a binary download (no 404).
Look for `""sprite"": ""https://my.cdn.com/sprites/basic""` (no extension).
Open `https://my.cdn.com/sprites/basic.json` – it should return a JSON object, and `basic.png` should be a 256 × 256+ PNG.
In the Network tab, click a glyph or sprite request → Headers → `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. It must include your page’s origin (or `*`).
In the TileJSON (or MBTiles/PMTiles metadata) look at `vector_layers`. You should see entries like `""id"": ""place""` or `""id"": ""road_label""`.
In the style, each `type: ""symbol""` layer must have `""source-layer"": ""place""` (or whatever the tile provides).

Symbol layers must be **above** the fill/line layers they label, but **below** any later‑added custom layers that you might be inserting on top of everything. Use `map.addLayer(..., beforeId)` to insert them correctly.

column1: If any of the above checks fails, you’ll see errors in the browser console such as:
Error: Failed to load glyphs for font ""Open Sans Regular""
Error: Sprite JSON not found at https://…/sprites/basic.json
Those messages are the clearest clue that the problem is missing glyphs/sprites.
## 3. Two typical scenarios & how to fix them
### Scenario A – You have a **complete vector tile source** (e.g. a Planetiler or OpenMapTiles basemap) but you never added glyphs/sprites to the style.
**Fix:** Add the glyphs and sprite URLs that match the tile schema. The OpenMapTiles project ships a ready‑made set you can host yourself or pull from a CDN.
/* IMPORTANT: keep the original label layers from the basemap */
*If you don’t want to host the fonts yourself, the OpenMapTiles CDN (`https://cdn.openmaptiles.org`) is free for public use (just respect the attribution).*
### Scenario B – You generated **your own tiles** (e.g. with tippecanoe) **without any label layers**.
Use a public basemap that already contains labels (OpenStreetMap, OpenFreeMap, Protomaps, etc.) and keep its label layers in the style, while using your own tiles for the data overlay.
/* Insert your own layers *before* the first label layer */
If you really need a *single* tileset (e.g. for offline PMTiles), add label features to the source before you run tippecanoe. Typical workflow:
1. **Merge** your data with a small OSM extract that contains only the label layers you need (`place`, `road_label`, `water_name`).
2. **Run tippecanoe** with `--layer=place --layer=road_label …` so those layers are kept.
3. **Serve** the resulting MBTiles/PMTiles file; the style can now reference those source‑layers directly.
## 4. Minimal working example (self‑hosted tiles + OpenMapTiles glyphs)
Below is a **complete style JSON** you can drop into `map.setStyle(styleUrlOrObject)` to see labels appear. Adjust the URLs to point at your own tile server.
// 👉 1️⃣ Glyphs – use the OpenMapTiles public CDN (or host your own)
// 👉 2️⃣ Sprite – same CDN provides a generic sprite sheet
// ---- Your data layers (insert *before* the first label layer) ----
// ---- Keep the original label layers from the tile source ----
// (these are the layers that actually draw the text)
// … add any other label layers you have …
* `glyphs` and `sprite` point to **publicly hosted assets** that already have CORS enabled.
* The `layers` array contains **both** your custom data layer (`my-points`) **and** the label layers (`place-label`, `road-label`).
If you generated your own tiles without those label layers, simply remove the label entries – the map will still render geometry but no text will appear (which is exactly what you’re seeing now).

* The label layers are placed **after** your custom layers, but **before** any later layers you might add at runtime. If you add layers later with `map.addLayer()`, pass the `beforeId` of the first label layer (or use `map.moveLayer()` to reorder).
## 5. Debugging workflow (what to look at in the browser)
1. **Open DevTools → Console** – look for errors that start with `Error: Failed to load glyphs` or `Sprite JSON not found`.
2. **Network tab → Filter “font”** – you should see requests like `.../fonts/Open%20Sans%20Regular/0-255.pbf`. If they are 404 or blocked, that’s the problem.
3. **Network tab → Filter “sprite”** – you should see `.../sprites/streets.json` and `.../sprites/streets.png`. Same 404/CORS check.

4. **Network tab → Tiles** – verify that the tile requests return **vector** (`application/x-protobuf`) and that the response includes the label layers (you can inspect a tile with the “Mapbox Vector Tile” viewer extension or by decoding it with `vt2geojson`).

5. **Style inspector (MapLibre GL JS “inspect” tool)** – click on a label layer in the style panel; it will show you the `source-layer` name and the fields it expects. If the source-layer is missing, the layer will be greyed out.

column3: Reason to switch
Parsing time becomes noticeable on low‑end devices.

column2: **Frequent updates** (e.g., dozens of stores added daily)
column3: Regenerating a static GeoJSON file each time is fine, but if you need *instant* propagation to many users you might prefer a tile server that can serve fresh tiles on demand.

column2: **Public CDN distribution** for a *very high* traffic site (hundreds of thousands of concurrent users)
column3: A static `.pmtiles` file on a CDN can serve many more requests per second than a single GeoJSON endpoint, because the browser caches individual tile ranges.

column3: Tippecanoe can generate vector tiles with built‑in clustering and simplification.

Add a second `heatmap` layer that reads the same GeoJSON source. Works fine for 50 points (just a visual effect).
